newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FUNDS, RUSSIAN WORRIES PUSHING PGM METALS HIGHER.
newsitem.headline: FUNDS, RUSSIAN WORRIES PUSHING PGM METALS HIGHER.

text.p: Attempts by U.S hedge funds to squeeze the platinum group metal (PGM) market and ongoing concern over Russian supplies were pushing already volatile platinum and palladium prices higher, analysts said on Thursday.
Platinum was fixed at $440.00 in London earlier, the white metal's highest level since September 15 1995, while palladium was fixed at $235 an ounce -- its highest ever.
BOE NatWest platinum analyst Paul Brogan said platinum was showing an obvious de-linking from the gold price while there was a shortage of palladium in the market.
On Thursday, platinum was trading at a premium of around $98 above gold while in the past it traditionally held about $20 above the yellow metal.

"Whilst there is an obvious physical shortage of palladium because the Russians aren't selling and they provide two-thirds of the world's palladium, it is not necessarily the case for platinum," Brogan said.
Brogan said he believed U.S hedge funds -- in particular New York-based Tiger Management -- was trying to squeeze the palladium market.
"I see in particular Tiger Management (trying to squeeze the market). They've got a stock of 1.5 million to 2 million ounces. That is enough to keep the market going for a couple of months.
"What they have been doing surreptiously, I am told, is offering 50,000 ounces in a lot to various consumers like Engelhard.

"They are not supplying it, they are leaking it into market. They are afraid that with such a huge amount of metal sitting on their books, the moment they start letting it out in any significant quantities, that price is going to take a bit of a dive and they won't make any profit out of it," Brogan said.
Analyst Ross Gardiner of stockbrokers SocGen Frankel Pollack said many commodity trading houses might have built up a stock of palladium since the beginning of the year.
"A lot of trading houses probably build up a stock at the beginning of the year and that caused even more tightness in the market," Gardiner said.
Brogan said Russia was also sitting on a stockpile of palladium which was growing because Russian output had not been cut back.
Gardiner and Brogan said the price of palladium was way above what they considered to be sustainable in the current market.
"As soon as the Russians or anybody else start supplying again, the price will take a huge and very sharp drop, I would guess down to $120-$130 an ounce," Brogan said.
This would drag platinum down, probably to a range of $380-$400 and ounce.

"Everything depends on the Russians, that is the key issue. Some people have said that they are going to supply again on June 22 and Johnson and Matthey have suggested that July is a good assumption," he added.
Concern about supply delays from Russia have caused PGM prices to surge in recent months.
But Japanese traders said such worries had been alleviated as ongoing 1997 term contract talks between Japanese clients and the Russian PGM export agency were progressing smoothly.
Japanese clients have been told by the Russians that exports would begin around June 20, and that Russia has enough supplies for all of its customers.
Russia is the world's biggest producer of palladium and is the world's second-largest platinum producer after South Africa.
